name: Microabrasion

lead: Microabrasion clears white or brown spots on the front teeth, including fluorosis marks, so the smile looks more even in colour. The change is visible right after the dentist polishes the tooth.

A mild acid and pumice take off a very thin layer of surface enamel, a few tenths of a millimetre, and the stain goes with it. The method dates to a 1986 technique by Croll and Cavanaugh, and recent clinical trials compare it with resin infiltration and other minimally invasive options.

paras: A dentist applies the acidic abrasive paste to the affected teeth in a single visit, rinses and polishes, and often finishes with a fluoride or protective step. People use it for mild to moderate fluorosis, enamel defects and white spots left after braces, sometimes alongside whitening afterward.

Enamel that is removed does not grow back, and over-thinning can let darker dentine show through. It does not reach stains that sit deep in dentine, such as tetracycline staining. It is carried out by a dentist, and anyone with already thin enamel is a poorer fit.

angle.text: Microabrasion clears white or brown spots, including fluorosis marks, so front teeth look more even in colour. A dentist removes a thin layer of stained enamel, and the surface change shows right after polishing. The method has been in clinical use since the 1980s.

lead: Enamel microabrasion is a cosmetic dental procedure that removes a very thin outer layer of enamel, using a mildly acidic abrasive compound, to reduce surface discolouration such as white or brown spots.[1] People use it to even out the colour of their front teeth, so that fluorosis mottling, post-braces white marks or developmental stains look less noticeable in a smile, without a veneer or crown.[1][2]

The first practical method, using weak hydrochloric acid and pumice, was developed by Theodore Croll and Richard Cavanaugh in 1986.[1] It is applied by a dentist, usually in one or a few short sessions, and is often described as a conservative option because it removes only a few tenths of a millimetre of enamel.[1][3]

It is used mainly for dental fluorosis and for enamel defects including white spot lesions after orthodontic appliances.[1][2] It is not suited to discolouration located in dentine, such as tetracycline staining.[1] Systematic reviews and registered clinical trials compare it with bleaching, resin infiltration and remineralising pastes.[4][5][6]
infobox: A few tenths of a millimetre[1]

paras: The procedure combines mechanical and chemical action to remove superficial enamel. A rubber dam is typically used to protect the gums and lips, which can be hard to place on teeth that have not fully erupted.[1] Before microabrasion, stained teeth were often covered with restorations such as porcelain veneers, which commonly needed later replacement.[1]

Variants differ in the acid and abrasive used. Hydrochloric acid with pumice is the original; a registered trial has compared it with sodium hypochlorite with pumice, and another registered trial is testing phosphoric acid and a proprietary paste against hydrochloric acid.[7][8] A related approach, microabrasion-remineralisation, follows the abrasion step with a calcium-phosphate product such as CPP-ACP (Tooth Mousse).[9]

A general encyclopedia article says microabrasion should be considered first for mild and moderate fluorosis.[1] It is also used for orthodontic-related defects and developmental enamel defects, and age is not a limiting factor.[1] Reviews of white spot lesions after orthodontic treatment discuss it among management options alongside fluoride, remineralising agents, bleaching and resin infiltration.[2][10]

It is not indicated when discolouration lies in dentine, as in dentinogenesis imperfecta or tetracycline staining, and partially erupted teeth can make isolation difficult.[1] The same source notes that treatment is better delayed where lip seal is deficient, because dry enamel makes stains more visible.[1]
Thinning enamel can expose dentine, which may look yellowish or darker, and bleaching can be combined to mask this.[1]

A 2023 systematic review of paediatric microabrasion (11 prospective studies, six randomised) concluded that it appears an effective and reliable technique for pre- and post-eruptive enamel discolouration, especially fluorosis, and called for more well-powered randomised studies for other spot types.[5]

A 2018 systematic review of dental fluorosis treatments (six randomised trials, 348 patients, mean age 17.7) found low-quality evidence that microabrasion gave a smaller aesthetic improvement than bleaching, and moderate-quality evidence that resin infiltration, alone or with bleaching, gave larger improvements than bleaching alone; the authors cautioned that each comparison rested on single trials.[4] A 2021 meta-analysis of resin infiltration (11 studies, 413 patients) reported its masking effect for white spot lesions and fluorosis.[6]

Clinicians writing about the technique in the 1990s and 2000s reported that certain patients benefit most from combined microabrasion and bleaching, and described microscopic changes in treated enamel that carry clinical implications.[11] Laboratory and clinical work cited in the encyclopedia article suggests treated enamel can be smooth and, after fluoride paste, harder, and may resist demineralisation and bacterial colonisation better than untreated enamel.[1]

A review article gives an overview of clinical and scientific considerations of enamel microabrasion.[3] A 2012 comparative clinical trial examined whether white spot lesions can be treated effectively, and a 2013 trial compared microabrasion with a combined approach for fluorosed teeth.[12][13] A 2019 split-mouth randomised trial compared resin infiltration and microabrasion for post-orthodontic white spots.[14] A 2020 trial on 60 extracted teeth with white spots compared bleaching, resin infiltration and microabrasion on colour restoration, and a 2023 randomised trial of 171 teeth with incisor hypoplasia compared resin infiltration with microabrasion-remineralisation using two pastes.[15][9]

Registered trials include a completed 60-patient comparison of hydrochloric acid-pumice and sodium hypochlorite-pumice for fluorosis,[7] a 30-patient split-mouth comparison of resin infiltration and microabrasion for early lesions,[16] a 42-patient trial of resin infiltration versus microabrasion with CPP-ACP for fluorotic white spots,[17] and a trial comparing resin infiltration with a combined microabrasion approach for molar incisor hypomineralisation.[18] A recruiting trial of 60 participants compares acid options in microabrasion.[8] Outcome data from the registrations were not available.

The main consequence is the permanent loss of a small amount of enamel, which does not regrow.[1] Over-thinning can reveal underlying dentine and a more yellow shade.[1] Treated surfaces are often followed with fluoride or remineralising products to improve smoothness and hardness.[1][9]

Removal of the outermost enamel to reach an underlying, presumed unaffected layer was proposed in 1916.[1] R. J. McCloskey described a fluorosis stain-removal technique in 1984, and Croll and Cavanaugh published their controlled acid-pumice method in Quintessence International in 1986; Croll and Killian extended it to surface texture and decalcification defects in 1990.[1] A review published ten years after the method appeared described the refined protocol and long-term results.[11]

timeline.event: Removal of outermost enamel is first proposed.[1]
McCloskey describes a technique for removing fluorosis stains.[1]
Croll and Cavanaugh develop the hydrochloric acid and pumice method.[1]

Ten-year review of the technique is published.[11]
